implementation_notes: Go has no inheritance, so the base-decorator boilerplate disappears: embed the component interface as an anonymous field and every method of that interface is promoted to the wrapper automatically, leaving only the methods whose behaviour changes to be written. The standard library demonstrates it everywhere - bufio.Reader wraps an io.Reader and is itself an io.Reader, as do gzip.Reader, io.LimitReader and io.TeeReader - so chains such as gzip.NewReader(bufio.NewReader(f)) compose transparently. Embed the interface rather than a concrete struct so any implementation can be wrapped; this is the better variant when the decorated interface has several methods or the decorator carries configuration and state.

variants.name: Struct embedding the component interface (method promotion)
variants.idiom_name: struct{ Component } with the changed methods defined on the wrapper; all other methods are promoted from the embedded interface

The standard library demonstrates it everywhere - bufio.Reader wraps an io.Reader and is itself an io.Reader, as do gzip.Reader, io.LimitReader and io.TeeReader - so chains such as gzip.NewReader(bufio.NewReader(f)) compose transparently. Embed the interface rather than a concrete struct so any implementation can be wrapped; this is the better variant when the decorated interface has several methods or the decorator carries configuration and state.
pitfalls: An embedded interface holding nil compiles cleanly and panics on the first promoted call - a nil dereference reported at a line you never wrote.

Promotion is not virtual dispatch: if a promoted method calls another method of the interface, it calls the embedded implementation, never your override, because Go has no `super` and no back-dispatch to the outer type.

Embedding a concrete struct instead of the interface exports the whole inner API and locks the decorator to one implementation; wrapping http.ResponseWriter additionally drops optional interfaces (http.Flusher, http.Hijacker) unless they are re-implemented.

variants.name: Function middleware (func(Handler) Handler / func(Reader, Writer) style)
variants.idiom_name: higher-order function returning a wrapped http.HandlerFunc (or any func-typed contract) that calls next before/after its own work
variants.implementation_notes: For one-method contracts the community standard is a function, not a struct: `func(next http.Handler) http.Handler` returns a handler that does its work and calls `next.ServeHTTP(w, r)`, and stacking is composition - `WithLogging(WithAuth(routes()))` - with no allocation per layer beyond the closure. The same shape covers http.RoundTripper, io.Writer adaptors and any function type, and every router and middleware library interoperates with it. Prefer the embedding variant when the contract has several methods (one function would have to thread each method through) or when the decorator owns state that belongs to an object.
pitfalls: Composition order is the nesting order: WithLogging(logger, WithAuth(...)) runs logging outside authentication; reversing the composition silently reverses the pipeline semantics.
Per-request state must live in the closure or the request context - a middleware struct with mutable fields shared across requests races under concurrency.
Wrapping http.ResponseWriter hides the optional interfaces (Flusher, Hijacker, Pusher) and the status code unless the wrapper re-implements them and records the write.
